items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: There was a relief band lead to a wonderful flautist named Albert Soccaras.

ctx.x: I always had very little patience with someone who was illogical, so I lost patience with Bechet very quickly. I told him that I was going to stay to report to the social security at the time I was supposed to report. He told me that if I didn't come along with him, and the rest of the musicians, he would take me to the union. I told him that he could take it to the Federal court if he wished to do so, and started to walk out of his house, when he called me and said: "And another thing, give me my God damn…

I collected my social security, did a few gigs until Leon Abbey, whom I had gone to India with and who was now in New York, offered me a job at the Ubangi club which was now down town in a basement at the corner of 52nd Street and Broadway. This was the hardest job I ever had in New York. The band was small, consisting of piano, drums, trumpet, tenor sax, bass and violin. There was a relief band lead to a wonderful flautist named Albert Soccaras. At one time, Soccaras had been a member of Chick Webb's orchestra.…

Abbey's combo was the band that had to accompany a big revue and the violin was no help because there were only two instruments that could really play loud. They were the tenor and trumpet. We started at 9 every night and there were no nights off. We played dance music and two shows a night. The relief band played one hour after the first show and an hour before the second one. We finished the night at three o' clock.
